The Economics of Inference

Every new model generation has made training more expensive, but the more interesting shift is happening on the inference side. When a model is used by hundreds of millions of people, the cost of serving it dominates the cost of building it, and that changes which companies win. The firms with the cheapest inference, not the best benchmark scores, end up setting prices for everyone else in the market.

Consider the economics from first principles. A training run is a fixed cost that is amortized over every query the model ever answers. Inference is a variable cost that scales with usage. If usage grows faster than model quality, the variable cost becomes the business. This is why the largest providers spend so much on custom silicon, and why the hyperscalers are willing to subsidize prices for years to capture usage.

There is a second-order effect that is easy to miss. Cheaper inference makes longer reasoning economical, which raises quality, which raises usage, which pushes inference volume higher again. The loop rewards whoever controls the full stack, from chips to data centers to the model itself, and it punishes companies that rent every layer of it from someone else.

That loop explains a lot of recent strategy: vertical integration, long-term power contracts, and the sudden interest in nuclear. It also explains why pricing pages change every quarter, and why application companies keep re-negotiating their contracts with model providers. The margin is moving, and everyone is trying to stand where it lands.

None of this means the winners are already decided. Distribution, product taste and enterprise trust still matter enormously, and a company that owns the customer relationship can switch model vendors faster than a vendor can win a customer.
